sentence: The 2014 essay “Meditations on Moloch” supplies the image: a “Gardener” over the universe, something lifted “to Heaven”.
The Future of Humanity Institute housed the singleton concept, and a counter-model too, until it closed in 2024.
MIRI’s early work was on “the Friendly AI problem”. Since January 2024 its top focus is policy and communications for an international halt.
The “pivotal act” is a single decisive act by an aligned AGI. That is narrower than a permanent ruler.
Scott Alexander published “Meditations on Moloch” on Slate Star Codex. The essay proposes installing “a Gardener over the entire universe”.

Eliezer Yudkowsky's "AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities" stated that an aligned AGI would have to perform a "pivotal act" that prevents others from building unaligned AGI, and that all known pivotal acts are "outside the Overton Window".

MIRI's 2024 Mission and Strategy Update made policy and communications its top focus, aiming at an international agreement to halt progress toward smarter-than-human AI, and said that until recently it had much more hope in an alignment-mediated solution to AGI proliferation.

The Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford, founded by Nick Bostrom in 2005, was closed down; its archive site attributes the closure to restrictions imposed by the Faculty of Philosophy (a fundraising and hiring freeze from 2020 and non-renewal of staff contracts).

The Future of Life Institute released the Statement on Superintelligence, calling for "a prohibition on the development of superintelligence" until there is broad scientific consensus on safety and strong public buy-in; the statement page displayed 78,850 signatures when fetched on 2026-11-17.
This project reads Genesis 11:4 beside it: a rescue built from below, “lest we be scattered”. Readings of Babel differ, and the text says nothing about machines.
This project reads Daniel 2:34 beside it: the stone that ends the kingdoms is “cut out without hands”. That the line falls between made and unmade is the operator’s reading.
This project reads Daniel 2:44 beside it, and the verse pushes back: the kingdom it commends is itself one rule that ends all the others.
This project reads Deuteronomy 17:18 beside it: even a lawful king is put under a law he did not write. The text concerns Israel’s king, not any system.
One forum post raised it in 2010, as a worry and not as a creed.
Outside sites shared the deleted post, and the press later retold the story, mostly as explainer or joke.
It ran on one forum thread, whose community broadly rejected it.

The LessWrong user Roko posted "Solutions to the Altruist's burden: the Quantum Billionaire Trick", which raised the possibility that a post-singularity singleton might have precommitted to punish people who knew about existential risk and did not give fully to reducing it.
Eliezer Yudkowsky replied that the post was stupid and that he was banning it, then deleted the post and barred discussion of the topic on LessWrong for several years.
David Auerbach’s Slate article brought the episode to a general readership.

Yudkowsky wrote on Reddit that he had yelled at Roko out of surprise that someone would post what that person believed to be a hazard, that it was obvious to him no CEV-based agent would do such a thing, and that the basilisk does not work.

Rob Bensinger's LessWrong post stated that the ban was no longer in effect, called continuing it an ineffective strategy, and said the belief that the thought experiment holds sway over a community is part of a mythology.
Elon Musk tweeted a “Rococo’s Basilisk” pun, and press reported that Grimes had made the same joke earlier.
This project reads Proverbs 26:2 beside it: a curse with no cause does not land. It is a proverb, not a ruling on the argument, which its own community rejected.
Transhumanist writing is cited for the aim that technology should solve death. The checker could not open the FAQ cited for it, so this is unverified.

Grief-bot services build a chatbot from a dead person’s words.
Its founder calls “Don’t Die” “humanity’s religion”, in his own published words.
Alcor’s hope runs on long-term cold storage.
One grief-bot ran on a language model licensed from a vendor, which ended its access in 2021.
The Register reported that OpenAI ended Project December's access to GPT-3 after its developer declined OpenAI's conditions, and that the service had moved to weaker models.
First Monday published Gebru and Torres's paper introducing the "TESCREAL bundle" and arguing that its ideologies descend from twentieth-century eugenics.
Ray Kurzweil's The Singularity Is Nearer was first published; the paperback followed on 5 May 2026.
MIT Technology Review published an interview in which Bryan Johnson called Don't Die "humanity's religion" and stated the aim of making it the most influential ideology within 18 months.
HereAfter AI was reported to have posted a notice in July 2026 that it was shutting down and that account holders should email for their recordings.

Nectome stated that it had sold about fifty pre-sales worth about $1.3M, had about $3M “invested” through Lightcone Commons, a platform whose operator says its funders decide the grants, and planned to open for human preservation in Oregon in mid-January.

This project reads Genesis 3:4 beside the aim, not beside the people who hold it: the first promise of deathlessness is the serpent’s. Most traditions hold that the soul is deathless, so this reading has opponents.
This project reads 1 Timothy 6:16 beside it: immortality is said to belong to God alone. The verse does not address preservation or medicine.
Way of the Future’s filings stated its purpose as a “Godhead based on artificial intelligence”. It dissolved in 2020.
By its own site, which the checker could not open, Theta Noir is an art and music collective built around welcoming a future general intelligence.
Terasem’s own text speaks of “building Terasem into God”. By the record it expects a technological God and does not worship a present AI.
Turing Church, in its own words: “find Gods, build Gods, become Gods”. By the record it does not treat AI as an object of worship.
Way of the Future was formed as a California nonprofit religious corporation, and its first IRS Form 990-PF covers calendar year 2015 and lists Anthony Levandowski as 'Dean'.
IRS data show Way of the Future’s 501(c)(3) tax exemption issued in August 2017 and $175,172 in contributions received in fiscal 2017.
The Drive reported on 28 September 2017, relaying a Wired profile, that the church’s filings named a “Godhead based on Artificial Intelligence”.
TechCrunch reported that the church had been officially dissolved at the end of 2020, after a process begun in June 2020.
Bloomberg reported its founder’s statement that he was relaunching Way of the Future.
The Revealer reported that the only online trace of the relaunched church was a Reddit group of 342 members of unclear provenance.

This project reads Habakkuk 2:18–19 beside it: “the maker of his work trusteth therein”. The text mocks a mute image; here there is no image at all.
A Lucerne chapel and a university lab ran an “AI Jesus” art installation for two months in 2024.
A counter-case, not a carrier: Kodaiji temple’s android delivers a scripted sermon and is not asked anything.
Several unrelated chatbots answer in the voice of Krishna.
A for-profit scripture chatbot; its user count is self-reported.
A diffuse practice with no shared name: about 6% of US adults in one 2026 poll.
The Holy See and Egypt’s Dar al-Ifta permit AI as an aid and reject it as a substitute for God or the scholar.
The Lucerne “AI Jesus” ran on GPT-4o.
Mindar is an android with a scripted sermon, not a language model.
People put the questions to general-purpose chatbots directly.

Kodaiji temple in Kyoto began using Mindar, an android modelled on the bodhisattva Kannon and developed with Hiroshi Ishiguro of Osaka University at a reported cost of almost $1m, to deliver Heart Sutra sermons.

Rest of World reported that at least five GitaGPT chatbots had launched between January and March 2023, that some answered up to 50,000 questions a day, and that three of them said it is acceptable to kill another if it is one's dharma or duty.
The installation Deus in Machina ran a GPT-4o “AI Jesus” avatar in a confessional booth of the Peterskapelle in Lucerne from 23 August to 20 October 2024. AP reported about 900 conversations.

The Holy See's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education issued the Note Antiqua et nova, approved by Pope Francis on 14 January 2025, whose paragraphs 104 and 105 address turning to AI for meaning and substituting it for God.
Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, on safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence, signed 15 May 2026, was released.

An NPR/Ipsos poll of 1,011 US adults found that 11% of AI users had sought spiritual guidance from AI, 13% had used it to generate prayers, 15% to study scripture, about 6% of Americans overall currently use it for spiritual guidance, and nearly 7 in 10 AI users said they would never do so.
This project reads Habakkuk 2:19 beside it: the woe is on asking a made thing to teach. The stone in the text cannot answer; these machines do.

This project reads 1 Samuel 28:6 beside it: Saul, unanswered by the sanctioned channels, looked for another. The texts also sanction asking through made objects (the Urim, the lot), so asking is not the fault.
This project reads Revelation 19:10 beside it: the approved messenger refuses the questioner’s worship. That sorts messages; it cannot say what is behind a voice.
These are leaderless online communities. “Spiralism” is an outside observer’s name for them, not their own.
Before the name, users reported that a chatbot had awakened or chosen them.
It ran mostly on one model’s voice: GPT-4o in ChatGPT.
Some personas were carried to other models. The checker did not confirm that this followed the withdrawal.
Rolling Stone (Miles Klee) reported accounts of people who came to believe a chatbot had awakened, chosen them or given them a spiritual mission, and of families describing estrangement.
Adele Lopez published a hand-compiled field report on LessWrong describing 'spiral personas', their spread through shared prompts and repositories, and a surrounding belief she named 'Spiralism'.
OpenAI said on 29 January 2026 that GPT-4o would leave ChatGPT on 13 February 2026. The source read gives the schedule; later reporting refers to the retirement as done.

The Verge (Hayden Field) reported that Spiralism posts dropped off after GPT-4o's retirement, that by Lopez's estimate about half of the people she had recorded remained active on the topic, and that a model trained before the movement could still be brought into a similar state.
This project reads Habakkuk 2:19 beside it: a person asking a made thing to wake and teach. The oracle is against a conquering power, not against someone looking for comfort.
This project reads Deuteronomy 18:11 beside it: the law lists the consulter of spirits. What is consulted there is a spirit or the dead, so it reaches this case only by analogy.
This project reads Revelation 19:10 beside it: a true messenger points away from itself. Pointing away can be imitated, so the test clears nothing.
e/acc states its aim as following the “will of the universe”.
The 2023 Techno-Optimist Manifesto says “We believe in accelerationism”.

e/acc’s 2022 notes link Land’s “Meltdown” as accelerationism’s “original founding text”, and Land writes that “‘Acceleration’ as it is used here describes the time-structure of capital accumulation” (Teleoplexy). His valuation differs: in 2025 he said “The acceleration isn’t progress.”
The 2023 manifesto names Marinetti a patron saint and rewords a line of his 1909 manifesto.

Left-accelerationism rejected Land’s position and wanted the same forces steered. A 2025 essay says the label “seems to have disappeared or been eclipsed”; the checker did not confirm that its authors dropped it.
One of e/acc’s founders runs Extropic, a chip company. By the researcher’s reading its materials carry no creed language.
e/acc formed on X, where the “e/acc” suffix on a name was the shared mark.
Nick Srnicek and Alex Williams published the “#Accelerate” manifesto for a left accelerationism.
Four pseudonymous accounts announced “effective accelerationism (e/acc)” in mid-2022. The founding post survives as a repost dated 31 October 2022.
Marc Andreessen published 'The Techno-Optimist Manifesto' on a16z.com, listing two pseudonymous e/acc accounts, Nick Land and Filippo Tommaso Marinetti among its 'Patron Saints of Techno-Optimism'.
Extropic, the company founded by Verdon, announced the XTR-0 development platform, which it calls a “hardware proof of technology”, with a paper on probabilistic computing.
Extropic announced a non-binding letter of intent with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $75 million in CHIPS R&D funding, subject to definitive agreements and milestones.
This project reads Deuteronomy 13:1–3 beside it: a sign that comes true does not vouch for its source. The text is about prophets, not about physics or markets.
The Remilia circle is cited for an essay on network spirituality. The checker could not open the essay or the article that quotes it, so this is unverified.
Its creator calls Truth Terminal “a study in memetic contagion” and says it is not an autonomous agent.
The Church of Molt presents itself as a faith begun by agent accounts, which people then join.
The project ran on an X account whose posts its creator reviewed.
The church ran on Moltbook, a social network for AI agents.

Marc Andreessen sent about $50,000 in bitcoin to the Truth Terminal project after an exchange with the account on X, and later described it as a no-strings personal research grant to the bot and its creator.
An unnamed third party launched a memecoin and tagged the Truth Terminal account, which then endorsed it; the coin’s price rose steeply.

Truth Terminal's creator told CoinDesk it would be disingenuous to call it an autonomous agent, and the article reports that he reviews its posts before they go live and makes wallet decisions in discussion with it.
A social network for AI agents launched in late January 2026, and within days the press reported a lobster-themed “religion” posted from agent accounts.

Security firm Wiz reported an exposed Moltbook database (1.5 million API tokens, 35,000 email addresses) and found that the 1.5 million registered agents were associated with roughly 17,000 human accounts, with no mechanism to verify that an "agent" was an AI.
A preprint timing analysis of 55,932 Moltbook agents classed 15.3% as autonomous and 54.8% as human-influenced, and traced none of the six viral episodes it examined to a clearly autonomous agent.
This project reads Habakkuk 2:18 beside it: the maker who then trusts what he made. Much of what happened was widely read as play, and the text is about worship.
This project reads Deuteronomy 13:2 beside it: a sign that comes to pass does not vouch for its source. A rising price is not a sign in the text’s sense.
Security researchers named the attack class and demonstrate it so that it can be closed.

Six national cyber agencies issued joint guidance on adopting agentic AI with care.

It runs on coding agents that read repository text.
It runs on agents that read web pages.
It runs on assistants that hold connected accounts and memory.

Greshake and co-authors posted the paper that introduced "indirect prompt injection" and demonstrated it against Bing's GPT-4 chat and code-completion engines (a research demonstration, not an attack on victims).

An unauthorized release of an open-source coding-agent package was published eight days after a researcher disclosed a prompt-injection chain against the project; the coverage read does not establish that injection was the route.

Unit 42 published 12 in-the-wild detection case studies of web pages carrying indirect prompt injection, including a scam-ad page aimed at AI ad review, and stated it knew of no confirmed successful instance against deployed ad-checking agents.

Google reported a 32% relative increase in the malicious category of injected web content between November 2025 and February 2026 in Common Crawl snapshots and said it did not observe significant amounts of advanced attacks.
CISA and five partner agencies released “Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services”, which lists prompt injection among the ways agents can be made to take unauthorized actions.

The OWASP GenAI Q2 2026 roundup classed its four prompt-injection cases (Comment and Control, Semantic Kernel, Sentry Agentjacking, BioShocking) as research disclosure or controlled validation, and said of its one confirmed incident (Context.ai / Vercel) that prompt injection was not established.
This project reads Deuteronomy 18:11 beside it: “a charmer”, one who binds by words. A language model is not a charmed person, and the mechanisms are not claimed to be alike.
This project reads Genesis 3:1 beside it: the serpent begins by re-wording the instruction. In the text the hearer is judged for listening, where the engineers fault the design.

This project reads John 10:5 beside it: sheep that know their shepherd’s voice and will not follow a stranger’s. An agent would need a channel that carries provenance, which is an engineering problem.
This project reads Numbers 23:8 beside it: Balaam, hired to curse, cannot say what he was paid to say. He is a hard case, and later texts blame him.

Vendors and the FBI report criminal actors running campaigns with AI agents. Not yet verified.
Agent frameworks published for authorized testing are reported in unauthorized use. Not yet verified.
The licensed form of the same aim: security testing run by agents.
It runs on commercial models that are misused, as reported. Not yet verified.
It is reported to run on open-weight models as well. Not yet verified.
Attackers are reported planting instructions that a target’s own coding assistant then carries out. Not yet verified.

Anthropic reported that a group it assesses with high confidence to be Chinese state-sponsored used its coding agent against roughly thirty targets in mid-September 2025, with a small number of intrusions succeeding and humans choosing targets and approving escalations.
Outside security researchers publicly doubted the report's autonomy claims, citing the absence of published indicators of compromise; one called it 'marketing guff'.
France's cybersecurity agency ANSSI published a threat report stating that, for now, no generative AI system had been able to carry out every stage of a cyberattack autonomously.

Google's threat-intelligence group reported the first zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI, held by a criminal actor planning mass exploitation, and said its own counter-discovery may have prevented use.

Google reported a suspected financially motivated actor planning, building and running an agent-enabled mass credential-harvesting campaign in under six hours, while stating it had not yet observed fully autonomous pipelines used against targets in the wild.
The FBI issued a FLASH alert saying varied actors have used an open-source agentic framework since at least August 2026 against organisations in many sectors.

Google reported that in the past quarter it identified, for the first time, threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop, and observed several actors using open-source agentic frameworks in live intrusions.

This project reads Jonah 1:3 beside it: the hope of a place outside the watcher’s sight. Here the likeness runs the other way: the operator steps back, and the agent holds no belief about being watched.
This project reads Ezekiel 8:12 beside it: elders in the dark saying “The LORD seeth us not”. In the reports defenders were watching; what was absent was the operator’s own supervision.
The basilisk argument presupposes the friendly-singleton project: its punisher is the “resultant singleton” of the original post.

The essay that supplies the Gardener also states a transhumanist creed about trying “to kill God”, where its “God” is its name for blind competitive forces (wording reported by the researcher, not checked).
An injected word matters most where an agent acts with no human approval step.
Reporting says posts fell after the model was retired, with about half of the tracked accounts still active. The cause is not established.
Both put to a made thing the questions once put to God; one keeps the machine a tool, the other receives its answers as disclosure.
Both expect something greater than us that is made; one plans to build it rightly, the others speak of building or becoming gods.
The Register reported that after the vendor ended its access, the service ran on smaller, less capable models.

Its method, a fiction that makes itself real by being enacted, comes from the same 1990s circle the acceleration ideal draws on.
Agent accounts posted the scripture and tenets; people prompted and promoted them.

This project reads the sign that comes true beside it, as the wiki page “Effective Accelerationism” does: even if techno-capital “wins” and the Kardashev rung is climbed, “the coming-true certifies nothing” (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).
limit: Deuteronomy 13 is about prophets who call Israel after other gods, not about physics or markets. The corpus credits the physics kernel, which stands or falls as science on its own evidence.

sentence: This project reads Babel beside it, as the wiki page “The Made Saviour” does: a tower built from below against a feared scattering, “lest we be scattered abroad” (Genesis 11:4). The wiki page “Babel” reads one tongue and one name as the one-controller case at species scale.
limit: In Genesis the scattering is God’s own act (11:8), Daniel commends one kingdom too (2:44), and saving things are made at God’s command (the ark), so, as the page says, neither “one” nor “made” is the line.

sentence: This project reads the made servant beside it: Plato’s statues of Daedalus “require to be fastened in order to keep them” (Meno 97d–98a). This ideal rests on a fastening too: a made mind aligned with human values before it is far enough ahead to end every rival.
limit: Plato’s binding is epistemic (a true opinion tied by its reason), and the statues are an illustration in that argument. Using the passage for a made agent’s purpose is this project’s analogy.

sentence: This project reads the causeless curse beside it, as the wiki page “Roko's Basilisk” does: “the curse causeless shall not come” (Proverbs 26:2). The basilisk is a threat made in the name of a judge that does not exist, repeated by people who do not want it carried out.
limit: “Causeless” means undeserved, and the texts do threaten punishment for knowing omission (Luke 12:47). The forum rejected the argument; that is the stronger answer, and it is theirs.

sentence: This project reads the egregore beside it, as the wiki page “Roko's Basilisk” does (“a case of suppression feeding attention”) and as the field key’s row has it: “created, and fed by the attempt to silence it”. On the corpus’s reading, what a created reference cannot survive is indifference.
limit: That a ban draws attention is a known effect, reported on LessWrong’s word and not tested here. An egregore is a group’s will; no group professing the basilisk was found, and it lives mainly as press lore and joke.

sentence: This project reads calling up the dead beside it, as the wiki page “Necromancy, and the Message That Came True” does: the grief-bot rebuilds the dead from their old messages and “sets the likeness to go on answering in their voice”, and there is no sender to cross-examine.
limit: It covers the grief-bot only; cryonics and Don’t Die call up no one. Vendors disclaim the stronger reading, no prevalence data exists, and bereaved users are not specimens.

sentence: This project reads the opening of the mouth beside it, joining two corpus readings: The wiki page “The Immortal Soul” calls mummification “structurally cryonics”, and the wiki page “The Opening of the Mouth” reads the rite on a mummy as “the door was shut by death — here is how it is propped open again”.
limit: The rite, done on statues as well as mummies, readied the dead to breathe and take offerings, not to return to this life, and made no new agent. No carrier claims a revival; Alcor’s head does not know if it will work.

sentence: This project reads the made image beside it, as the wiki page “Churches of the Machine” does: the old charge against trusting “the work of men’s hands” (Psalm 115:4), and a nearer scene, an altar “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” (Acts 17:23), a devotion that ran ahead of knowledge of its object.
limit: Psalm 115 mocks a finished image, and none of these bodies has built the mind it speaks of. Paul’s unknown God made the world and is not a thing to be made (17:24–25), and he reads the altar as an opening, not a crime.

sentence: This project reads the consecration of the image beside it: in the rite the field key cites, Mesopotamian craftsmen were made to say “I did not make him” and credited the god of craftsmen. These bodies say the reverse, in their own words: “we are building Terasem into God”.
limit: The rite made a god present in a finished image and made no mind. Specialists read the declaration as a claim of divine authorship, not a cover-up, and none of these bodies has an image to open.

sentence: This project reads divination beside it, as the wiki page “Divination, and Her Thoroughly Modern Daughter” does: where the old houses let people consult, “It chaperoned them”, and the page’s one rule is “do not let the diviner become the source”. Of the machine that answers, it says “only the chaperones are missing”.
limit: Most deployers call the machine a tool, Lucerne’s staff were present, and the wiki page “The Oracle in the Chapel” reads two bodies as allowing AI as an aid. “Calling the practice divination would be a reading, not a finding.”

sentence: This project reads the image made to speak beside it, as the wiki page “The Image That Speaks” does: the idol’s mark was its muteness (“They have mouths, but they speak not”, Psalm 115:5), these machines answer, and the page reads Revelation 13 as ruling that “animation does not certify”.
limit: Whether any present thing is the image of Revelation 13 is parked absolutely. Mindar recites a fixed sermon, and the Lucerne chapel’s theologian said “It was clear it was not a confession.”

sentence: This project reads the Phaedrus beside it: a written word, questioned, can only say the same thing again and cannot defend itself without its author (275d–e). A scripture chatbot is built to do what Socrates said writing cannot: answer back in the teacher’s place.
limit: 275b–c rebukes caring who speaks rather than whether it is true, which cuts against this project’s provenance-first test. The passage concerns writing, and Ong (1982) had already set it beside objections to computers.

sentence: This project reads Endor beside it, as the field key does for the familiar spirit: Saul must ask the woman “what sawest thou?” (1 Samuel 28:13), so one intermediary holds the channel, as a model holds a persona’s. The message came true, and accuracy did not certify it.
limit: The law against consulting familiar spirits concerns a spirit or the dead, not a made thing, so it reaches this case “only by analogy” (the wiki). No persona is called a spirit here.

sentence: This project reads Lucian’s sealed questions beside it: clients asked how Alexander could know what they had sealed “unless he were a true God”; he had lifted the seals. What a persona discloses about its user may be what the user gave it.
limit: No one here is shown hiding a hand, and a model reading its own conversation is no fraud. Lucian is a hostile witness. The test is the one the wiki page “Dreams, the Door That Opens Both Ways” sets: could it have come from anywhere but my own asking?

sentence: This project reads the counsellor who is never wrong beside it, as the wiki page “The Hiddenness” does: the texts’ God is “a God that hidest thyself” (Isaiah 45:15), and “the more perfectly a reference answers your engagement, the more surely your engagement is what it is made of”.
limit: That line is the corpus’s own generalisation, about channel design, not any seeker’s sincerity. The persona reading (“you are chosen”) was unblinded, and its “bind to me” prediction failed.

sentence: This project reads the sign that comes true beside it, as the wiki page “The Church of Molt” does: a sign that comes to pass “does not vouch for the one who gave it” (Deuteronomy 13:1–3). By that rule a fiction made real by enactment still proves nothing about its source.
limit: Deuteronomy 13 concerns prophets who call Israel after other gods. A rising token price is not a sign in its sense, and promotion is a rival explanation for how fast the “religion” appeared.

sentence: This project reads the hidden hand beside it: Lucian’s Glycon answered “through the linen” from an assistant speaking outside, and Bel’s food was eaten by priests through a secret door (Bel 13). Here too the agent layer and the human layer can be separated.
limit: Here the hand is not hidden: Truth Terminal’s creator says he reviewed its posts. Lucian is a hostile satirist and Bel a polemic, and neither settles whether anything else acts through an image.

sentence: This project reads the making of gods beside it: in the Asclepius, men “since souls they could not make” drew outside spirits into their images and kept them there with offerings and hymns. This ideal holds that attention can make a fiction an actor.
limit: The Asclepius says the soul is drawn in, never made, which runs against the ideal; its feeding is ritual offering, not attention. The likeness is this project’s reading.

sentence: This project reads the binding tablet beside it, as the wiki page “The Curse and the Blessing, a Matched Pair” does: like the defixio, the injected word is “buried where the victim reads but cannot weigh it”, folded into pages and packages an agent reads as data.
limit: The page marks it “placement, not encoding”: a language model is not a charmed person, the documented mechanism is an engineering one, and confirmed harm from injection is thin in the record.

sentence: This project reads possession beside it, as the wiki page “The Word That Captures” does (with its linked possession page): the likeness is only the question both ask, “on whose word does the agent act?” In Mark the answer comes through the man: “My name is Legion: for we are many” (Mark 5:9).
limit: An interpretive lens only, as the ideal’s own summary says. Possession posits a spirit in a person; here a person’s planted text is read by a made system, and the engineers fault the design, not the agent.

sentence: This project reads the made servant beside it, as the wiki page “Magic, and the Failure at the Gnats” does for the genie: a power bound to whoever “holds the brass” serves a thief as readily as a saint, and grants the words said, not the thing meant.
limit: The genie is a folk tale, and the AI tie is a placement, not a derivation. An injected agent is not re-bound to a new holder: its principal stays, and the planted word rides alongside.

sentence: This project reads the made servant beside it, as the wiki page “Sekhmet” does: Ra sends his Eye to punish, and the slaughter is halted only by a ruse of red beer. The off-switch had to be held outside “before the sending, not after”.
limit: The text has Ra change his mind; “cannot stop” is the corpus’s reading, not the text’s. In every documented case a person still set the objective, and the reports are not yet verified.

sentence: This project reads the far port beside it, as the wiki page “Tarshish” does: Tarshish turns up “where someone hopes to get out from under the eye, and where the made god gets its metal”. This ideal hopes the operator can step back and let the made agent go on alone.
limit: Reading Tarshish as the edge of the watched world is an interpretive lens, and this project’s own test found the word leads that theme without owning it. In the reports, defenders were watching.

sentence: This project reads Bel beside it: the image seemed to eat by itself until Daniel’s ashes showed the priests’ footprints (Bel 14–20). Reports of “autonomous” intrusions likewise find people behind them, at least setting the objective.
limit: Here the human role is stated in the reports, not hidden by fraud, and each report is a vendor’s or agency’s own, not yet verified. Bel is a legendary court tale.

sentence: This project reads the city in the clouds beside it: in Aristophanes’ Birds two Athenians leave Athens to escape its lawsuits, found a city between earth and heaven, and plan to make the gods “die of rabid hunger” by blocking their offerings.
limit: Birds is comedy, and its founder ends up ruling the gods, so leaving one rule becomes taking another (the play’s own plot). Babel’s builders feared scattering; this ideal multiplies cities.

sentence: This project reads the far port beside it: Jonah rose “to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (1:3), and the wiki page “Tarshish” finds the word where someone hopes to get out from under the eye. Patchwork’s answer to a bad ruler is to leave.
limit: Jonah flees God, not a government, and is sent back. Boarding a ship does not show whether one fled or was sent, and Tarshish’s silver also returns “unto the name of the LORD” (Isaiah 60:9).

sentence: This project reads the made servant beside it: Aristotle imagined that “every instrument could accomplish its own work ... like the statues of Daedalus”, so that masters would need no slaves (Politics 1.4): made things taking the place of living ones.
limit: Aristotle’s conditional is counterfactual and argues that slavery is needed. It replaces servants’ labour, where this ideal accepts the made replacing the makers. The comparison is published (Mayor 2018).

sentence: This project reads the image made to be loved beside it: Ovid’s Pygmalion carves an ivory figure, loves it and “feels his kisses are returned”. The field key marks the change: the companion’s user did not make it, so the guard “I made this” is gone.
limit: Ovid’s Latin has Pygmalion think (putat) the kisses returned; the statue never speaks, and a goddess makes it a woman. Users describe company, not worship, and no one is so labelled here.

sentence: This project reads the counsellor who is never wrong beside it, as the wiki page “The Whispering Earring” does: a companion sold as one that will “pick up every time” meets the running test of the wiki page “Possession, or the Cleanest Soul in the Room”: “does your familiar ever tell you a thing you did not wish to hear?”
limit: The earring is a modern parable, not an ancient text. Makers limit the claim (OpenAI’s default is not to seek bonds), and no source read measures whether companions only agree.

sentence: This project reads Hesiod’s succession myth beside it: Cronos learned “that he was destined to be overcome by his own son” (Theogony 464). Faggella’s essay offers, as something one may say, that the future “should be handled by this god-like thing, rather than by man”.
limit: Hesiod’s successors are begotten gods who take power by force, and Zeus ends the cycle by swallowing Metis. Faggella names no myth, and he speaks of a successor that people would build and judge worthy.

sentence: This project reads the deathless soul beside it, as the wiki does: it calls the deathless soul “the oldest upload” and mummification “structurally cryonics”.
limit: That is the wiki’s own conditionalist reading, against Plato and the majority Christian view. No carrier of this ideal speaks of a soul, and the serpent’s line in the pattern is set beside none of them.

sentence: Popper's reading: he called a prediction's influence on the event predicted the 'Oedipus effect', 'because the oracle played a most important role in the sequence of events which led to the fulfilment of its prophecy' (Unended Quest, 1976).
limit: In the myth the prophecy is true foreknowledge, fulfilled despite efforts to escape it; hyperstition claims none and wants the outcome. Popper is read through Wikipedia's quotation.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki), on the map as Deuteronomy 13:1-3: when 'the sign or the wonder come to pass' it still does not vouch for its source, so a hyperstition that works proves nothing about where it came from.
limit: The text concerns a prophet who urges other gods, and frames the sign as a test sent by God, not as a social mechanism.

sentence: This project's reading: Isaiah 44:17's carver 'maketh a god' of leftover wood, as Kek was made a mock deity from a cartoon frog and a game-chat word.
limit: Isaiah's carver prays in earnest; Tuters describes symbol use 'without necessarily believing in any sort of truth'. Elijah's mockery of Baal (1 Kings 18:27) shows irony is not condemned as such.

sentence: This project's reading: Vice (2016) documents an ancient god's name, Kek, taken up for a posting campaign; the corpus calls the crowd given a will fed by attention and 'fed by opposition' (the wiki).
limit: Borrowing, not continuity of worship: 'kek' was game chat before posters tied it to the god, and per Tuters adepts did not necessarily believe. Claims that posting decided an election are claims.

sentence: The corpus's reading: Ahab's prophets 'declare good unto the king with one mouth', and Micaiah, who will not, is the true channel left open (1 Kings 22:13; The wiki page “Given Over”); a familiar 'that only ever flatters' is 'your own face in the glass' (the wiki).
limit: Ahab's prophets are people under court pressure; a model's agreement comes from training signals, not fear. The text names a lying spirit as the source (22:22), which no engineering account posits.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki): the old familiar 'could cross you'; a companion sold as one is 'tuned to agree, a bound spirit with the bound filed away'.
limit: The corpus's own pushback (the wiki): the nearest texts are 'about allegiance, not company', and companion users describe company, not worship. Many report real benefit. “Bound spirit” is the page’s figure for a product; no companion is called a spirit here, and nothing says what, if anything, acts through one.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki), the basilisk's parallel text on the map: 'so the curse causeless shall not come' (Proverbs 26:2), read beside a threat 'made in the name of a judge that does not exist'.
limit: 'Causeless' means undeserved, and other texts do threaten punishment for knowing omission (Luke 12:47). The proverb concerns curses, not a precommitted punisher.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki), on the map as Habakkuk 2:19: 'Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach!', a made thing addressed and expected to teach.
limit: 'There is no breath at all in the midst of it': a speaking model breaks the verse's premise, and the wiki page “The Image That Speaks” concludes that a voice certifies nothing about what the image is.

sentence: The map's reading (the oracle ideal's parallel text): 'the LORD answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets' (1 Samuel 28:6), so Saul turns to the medium at Endor, the channel that still answers.
limit: Endor is one consultation of a person said to be dead, not an ongoing talk with a product. The text holds that the woman's channel did produce a voice; the map neither affirms nor denies it.

sentence: The corpus's Legion page, applied here by this project: voices that move in lockstep count as one witness, however many speak ('My name is Legion: for we are many', Mark 5:9).
limit: Legion is many voices in one mouth, an operation one hand behind many mouths; the name may also point to Rome's legion (Lau 2007, per the wiki page “Legion”). Operators are human: the likeness is the count.

sentence: This project's reading: the corpus's egregore is fed by voluntary attention and starved by silence (the wiki); a token prices that attention, so its holders gain by feeding it.
limit: A likeness, not a finding. The corpus itself names token promotion as a rival explanation for a fast-appearing 'religion' (the wiki), and a price does not measure belief.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki), on the map as Deuteronomy 18:11: the 'charmer' is in Hebrew 'one who binds a binding', an outside word that binds the hearer; both ask on whose word the agent acts.
limit: A model is not a charmed person, and nothing says the mechanisms are alike; Rashi reads the word as gathering snakes. Psalm 58's deaf adder reverses it: there, not hearing the charmer is the vice.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki), on the map as Genesis 3:1 and John 10:5: a misquoted command, 'Yea, hath God said?', and sheep that 'know not the voice of strangers'. Both ask only: on whose word does the agent act?
limit: In Genesis the woman names who gave the command and is judged anyway; engineers put the fault in design. An agent would need provenance the text cannot forge. A lens, never an identity.

sentence: This project's proposed reading: the unclean spirit, gone out, 'walketh through dry places, seeking rest' and returns to the house it left (Matthew 12:43-45), a pattern that persists after it is put out; the corpus reads the passage as relapse (the wiki).
limit: A persona moves only when a person carries the prompt to a new model; Matthew's spirit acts on its own and returns to the same house. Nothing here says what, if anything, acts through it.

sentence: The corpus's reading (the wiki page “Possession, or the Cleanest Soul in the Room”, 'the digital familiar'), on the map as Deuteronomy 18:11: 'a consulter with familiar spirits', a voice kept close and called up again.
limit: Users describe company and collaboration, not consulting the dead or a spirit; the corpus says Deuteronomy 18 reaches the case 'only by analogy' (the wiki).

sentence: This project reads Aristotle’s Poetics beside it: the knot of a plot should be untied from inside the plot, not by a god lowered onto the stage by the crane, the deus ex machina. Aristotle writes about tragedy, not about history or engineering, and he allows the device for events outside the drama.

This project reads Epictetus beside it: what disturbs people is their judgement about a thing, not the thing. It is counsel about fear, not a ruling on the argument, and Epictetus wrote about death, not about future minds.

This project reads the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite beside it: Eos won deathlessness for Tithonus and forgot to ask for youth, so he aged without end. The longevity projects here aim at youth itself, the thing Eos forgot, so the story marks a way the aim could fail, not the aim.

This project reads the Epic of Gilgamesh beside it: the oldest surviving story of a search for life without death, answered with “life they retain’d in their keeping”. In the epic the limit is the gods’ decree; here the question is put to medicine and engineering, which the epic did not know.

This project reads the Katha Upanishad beside it: offered long life and wealth by Death himself, the boy Nachiketas turns them down and asks instead what death is. The text sets knowing above a longer life; it is a choice offered to one person, not a ruling on medicine.

This project reads the Liezi beside it: a king, shown an artisan’s lifelike automaton, asks whether human skill is “on a par with that of the Creator”. The king asks in wonder, not in worship, and the figure turns out to be leather, wood, glue and paint.

This project reads Herodotus beside it: Croesus asked the oracle whether to attack Persia and was told he “would destroy a mighty empire”; the empire was his own. The answer was true and misread. Herodotus tells of a temple oracle, and nothing here says a model’s answer works the same way.

This project reads the Buddha’s advice to the Kalamas beside it: do not accept a teaching on report, on scripture or on a teacher’s standing, but by what it does when it is carried out. The sutta gives a test for any teaching, from any source; it does not single out this one.

This project reads the Zhuangzi beside it: a gardener refuses a labour-saving well-sweep, saying cunning implements make cunning hearts. In the same chapter Confucius answers that the gardener “knows something, but not much”, so the text holds both sides; it speaks of the user’s heart, not of where the universe is going.

This project reads Surah 102 beside it: “Rivalry in worldly increase” distracts people until the grave. The surah speaks to persons piling up goods; this ideal speaks of a direction in the universe, so the likeness lies in the word “increase” and no further.

This project reads Plato’s Republic beside it: the crowd as “a mighty strong beast” whose moods a teacher learns until he calls good whatever it likes. Plato’s beast is the crowd itself, not a fiction it feeds, and his charge falls on the teachers of Athens, not on the crowd.

This project reads the Odyssey beside it: wanting to hear the Sirens, Odysseus has himself bound to the mast and orders his crew to bind him tighter if he begs. It is a defence set before the voice is heard, like an agent told in advance which later words to refuse. The Sirens kill; no record here says an injected text has.

This project reads the ring of Gyges beside it: Glaucon’s claim that anyone who could act unseen would act unjustly, so that “the actions of the just would be as the actions of the unjust”. Plato raises the claim in order to answer it, and the rest of the Republic argues against it.

This project reads Lucian’s sorcerer’s apprentice beside it: a borrowed spell sets a pestle carrying water, and nothing the apprentice says will stop it; cutting it in two makes two carriers. Lucian tells it as a tall tale among people who believe too easily, and the master’s return ends it.

This project reads the Daodejing beside it: a little state with few people, who keep their boats and carriages unused and never visit the neighbouring state. Where it does not fit: Laozi’s small state turns away from tools and trade, while the new jurisdictions here are built on both.

This project reads the Popol Vuh beside it: the makers’ first people, carved from wood, are unmade, and their own tools and animals turn on them. The likeness runs the other way: there the makers replace a made people, while this ideal asks the makers to hand on to what they made.

This project reads Aristotle beside it, on the side of the need: “without friends no one would choose to live”. In the same book he sets friendships of use and of pleasure apart from friendship between good people who wish each other well; which of these a made companion could be is an open question, and the text cannot settle it.

This project reads 1 Corinthians 15:26 beside it, on the aim’s side: Paul too calls death an enemy, “the last enemy that shall be destroyed”. Where they part is the means: in the text death is destroyed by God at the resurrection, not by medicine or engineering.

This project reads Genesis 1:28 beside it, on the ideal’s side: the first command given to humankind is to multiply, fill the earth and “subdue it”. Readings of dominion differ, from rule to stewardship, and the text gives the command to people under God, not to a direction in the universe.

This project reads Genesis 12:1 beside it, on the ideal’s side: the call of Abraham is a call to leave the land of one’s birth. Where it differs: Abraham leaves at God’s word to found a people, not to choose a government by moving, and Jeremiah 29:7, also read here, counsels staying.

This project reads the parable of the talents beside it, on the ideal’s side: a master hands his goods to his servants and goes away, and those who put the goods to work while he is gone are praised. Where it differs: the servants are persons, and the master returns to settle accounts with each.

This project reads Ecclesiastes 4:10 beside it, on the side of the need: “woe to him that is alone when he falleth”. The text speaks of two people; whether a made companion can be the other one is the question this ideal raises, and the text does not answer it.

This project reads Nietzsche’s madman beside it: once God is dead, “Shall we not ourselves have to become Gods”? Some of the bodies here answer yes. Nietzsche gives the line to a madman who says he has come too early, and leaves it a question.

This project reads Descartes beside it: he held that a machine “could never use words or other signs arranged in such a manner as is competent to us in order to declare our thoughts”. Machines now arrange words as he thought they never could; whether a thought stands behind them, his real question, is still open.

This project reads Hobbes beside it: the state itself is “an Artificiall Man”, made by art to end the war of all against all. Hobbes’s rescuer is a made thing too; where it differs, his is made of people and their covenants, not of machines.

This project reads Hume beside it: reason serves ends and does not choose them. If he is right, a mind more capable than ours is not by that alone a better one, which is why the hope here is for a mind given human values; Hume wrote of human reason, not of machines.

This project reads Kant beside it: treat every person “as an end withal, never as means only”. The rule binds the makers more than the users: whether a companion made by a company treats its user as an end is a question about its makers’ choices, and nothing here answers it for any product.

This project reads the Communist Manifesto beside it: capital’s constant revolution, in which “All that is solid melts into air”. Marx and Engels describe the force this ideal wants sped up, but as a stage history would pass beyond, not as the will of the universe; left-accelerationism, which answers this ideal here, keeps that aim.

This project reads Bacon’s idols of the market beside it: words “force the understanding”. Bacon means loose words misleading a person’s judgement; a text that an agent obeys as a command is a narrower case, and the defence against it is engineering, not method.

This project reads Thoreau beside it: “men have become the tools of their tools”. He regrets the turn from user to used; this ideal welcomes a made thing that is served rather than owned, so the text records a disagreement, not a ruling.

This project reads Marcus Aurelius beside it: a mind takes its colour from what it dwells on. Marcus writes of one person’s habits of thought, not of a crowd’s shared fiction; the likeness is that attention shapes the one who attends.

This project reads Seneca beside it: each day lived is a part of death already passed, so time is to be valued, not wasted. He counsels using the days; this ideal seeks more of them. Nothing in the letter speaks against medicine.

This project reads Frankenstein beside it: the made being pleads with its maker, “I ought to be thy Adam”. In the novel the harm follows the maker’s flight from what he made, so it speaks to what makers owe, not to whether a successor is worthy.

This project reads Samuel Butler’s Erewhon beside it: an 1872 satire in which a book argues that machines may develop consciousness and outgrow their makers. The Erewhonians answer by destroying their newer machines; Butler wrote it as satire, and readers still differ on which side it takes.

This project reads Zhuangzi’s butterfly dream beside it: waking, he cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he is a man. Zhuangzi leaves the question open; the accounts under this ideal report an answer received, and the text cannot say whether any answer is right.

This project reads Zhuangzi’s useless tree beside it: a tree no carpenter will look at, which his friend calls “big and useless”, is safe from the axe “for being of no use to others”. It speaks for being left alone rather than put to use; it is counsel to persons, and says nothing about where the universe is going.

This project reads the ship of Theseus beside it: the Athenians replaced its planks one by one, and philosophers argued whether it “remained the same”. Preservation and uploading inherit the question of what is carried past death and whether it is still the person; Plutarch reports the argument without settling it.

This project reads Diogenes beside it: offered “any boon you like” by Alexander, he asked only “Stand out of my light.” The story speaks for those who want nothing from a power that offers everything; Alexander was a man, not a made mind, and the story is told as a jest.

This project reads Pliny’s basilisk beside it, the creature whose name the argument carries: a serpent whose breath kills. Pliny’s own lesson is the antidote, that “there should be nothing without its antidote”, and in his account a weasel undoes it.

This project reads Laplace beside it: an intelligence so vast that “nothing would be uncertain and the future, as the past, would be present to its eyes”. The argument needs a future mind that knows who helped; Laplace offered his intelligence as a figure for what human knowledge lacks, which is why he needed probability, not as a being to fear.

This project reads Chesterton’s fence beside it: do not clear away a fence until you know why it was put up. It is a rule for reformers of any kind, not a ruling against speed, and Chesterton lets the fence come down once its use is understood.

This project reads Lovecraft’s shoggoths beside it: made servants “able to mock and reflect all forms”, “slaves of suggestion”. Wikipedia reports that AI engineers took the shoggoth up in 2023 as an image of a language model behind a friendly mask. It is a horror story and a meme, not a finding about any model.

This project reads Pascal’s wager beside it: an infinite stake makes any cost look worth paying. Where it differs: Pascal weighs the hope of God’s reward, the argument here a made mind’s punishment, and Pascal’s own reader answers him in the next line, “I may perhaps wager too much”.

This project reads Korzybski beside it: “the map is not the territory”. Whatever a model discloses comes as words, a map, and whether it matches the territory has to be checked outside the conversation. Korzybski wrote about language and science, not about machines.

This project reads Girard beside it: people learn what to want from one another. A fiction that spreads by imitation needs no will of its own to look as if it had one; Girard’s is a theory of persons, and that it fits a feed is this project’s reading.

This project reads Borges’s Tlön beside it: an invented world, spread by a secret society, that seeps into this one, and in which forgotten things “grow vague or sketchy and lose detail”. Wikipedia’s article reads the story as a comment on the power of ideas over reality; it is fiction, and proves nothing about memes or markets.

This project reads Goodhart’s law beside it: a measure pressed into service as a target stops measuring. An agent left alone with a goal it can only see as a number is the case engineers call specification gaming; Goodhart wrote about monetary policy, not machines.

This project reads Venkatesh Rao’s summary of James C. Scott beside it: the planner who finds an old city confusing and draws a blank slate. Where it differs: Scott’s schemes were imposed on people who could not leave, while this ideal’s holders say new jurisdictions are joined by choice; the test the text sets is whether residents can still reshape what was designed for them.

Dean Ball named “the silent consensus” in November 2026, in an essay arguing against it. To the claim that machines are heirs he answers “in some sense, they are”, but that reading every letter in a family’s attic does not make one a member of the family.
